name: The Dark Lands
overview: Between the North Lands and the Middle Lands, across narrow straits, two dark arms of forest, ridge and volcano curl round an inner sea, the Sea of Darkness. The Dark Lands were never one realm: men, orcs, goblins, trolls, ogres, giants and demons live here under rulers of their own, and none of them belongs to Volgan by nature. Aen's northern garrisons left behind the men who became Dondor; orcs and goblins of the iron hills marched in Volgan's armies in the First Age while other Dark Lands soldiers fought him under Edran, and in 2A 1388 Dondor's spearmen stood with men of the south and an elven company to close the Burning Gate of Nezer. Late in the Second Age the holds opened their passes and their deep ways to the Necromancer's hosts, and in the Third Age the Buried Wars between his garrisons and the free holds bled his strength away. In the Fourth Age, once the great invasions had ceased, orc warlords united the inner Dark Lands as Goldoroth around 4A 1452, the goblins of Burnikit learned to make powder from the volcano's fire and sold it to the orcs' siege forges, and Dondor and the sea orcs of Belonton swore the Dark Sea Accord in 4A 1604. In 4A 1748 the two sides keep an armed peace of raids, gifts, tribute and beacon-fires; the free holds, the troll king Smash, the giants behind their cairn-line and a demon lordship on the black south answer only to themselves, and Volgan's envoys court them all. Years in the data are one continuous count from the victory of Aen on the proposed lengths of the ages (First Age 1,675 years, Second Age 2,133, Third Age 1,260): 1A 1 is year 1, 2A 1 is 1,676, 3A 1 is 3,809 and 4A 1 is 5,069, so that the campaign year 4A 1748 is 6,816; every entry also carries its date in the Age-and-year form, which is the form the prose uses.

ages.name: The Garrisons and the Charts
ages.summary: Aenoran ships charted the Dark Lands' coasts and left chart names behind them, and the garrisons Aen's heirs kept on the Dondor plain stayed when the ships stopped coming; their descendants, worn into the speech of their orc neighbours, became the men of Dondor. The orc holds of the iron hills were already old.

ages.name: The Southern Burning
ages.summary: Volgan opened contacts with the powers of the Dark Lands and found orcs and goblins willing to march for him when he invaded Mirolon in 1A 1150, while other holds and the men of Dondor sent soldiers to the Grand Alliance under Rovek of Dondor, who knew Volgan's friends better than anyone; the Dark Lands fought on both sides at Dardan.

ages.name: The Raiding Centuries
ages.summary: After Volgan's banishment many orcs and goblins kept fighting in his name and the free Dark Lands fell back into turmoil; bands of the iron holds crossed the Northern Dark Strait to raid the North in the Raiding Years, while Dondor's spearmen marched south in 2A 1388 to close the Burning Gate of Nezer, and the holds fought the War of the Black Roads against the Necromancer's followers in the years after Volgan returned.

ages.name: The Opening of the Passes
ages.summary: As the Necromancer's wars spread, orc and goblin armies descended from the Dark Lands and rose from the deep ways underground; the goblin warrens under the Goldoroth Mountains opened their tunnels to his hosts in 2A 2110 and closed them again when he did not pay.

ages.name: The Buried Wars
ages.summary: The Necromancer relied on orc and goblin garrisons to hold Aenor, and between 3A 431 and 3A 690 the Buried Wars between his garrisons and the free holds of the Dark Lands cost him men he could not replace. The free holds learned to fight for no master, a lesson they have kept.

ages.name: The Warkingdom and the Accord
ages.summary: The great invasions of orcs and goblins ceased with the Fourth Age. Orc clans moved from the hills into the volcano country, Goldoroth was united around 4A 1452 and began its wars with Dondor, the goblins of Burnikit sold powder to its forges from 4A 1566, and the Dark Sea Accord of Dondor and Belonton has held against the warkingdom since 4A 1604.

countries.name: Goldoroth

founding.story: For three centuries orc clans had been moving out of the hills into the volcano country of the Goldoroth arm, fighting each other for the warm slopes, until in 4A 1452 Skarag of the Krumgul broke the last rival chief in the ring at Sungodor and the chiefs of the four clan blocs acclaimed him Warking. He moved his seat to the forge-city below the Fire-Mountain, and the orcs call the realm Gruzgoroth, though every chart in Aoaz writes it Goldoroth.

roots.story: The Volcano Clans did not begin at the Fire-Mountain. Their songs start in the iron hills, where the oldest orc holds were dug long before Aen, and they turn on one grief: the march to Dardan. In the second millennium of the First Age Volgan's envoys came into the hills with gifts and promises, and the four great clan-lines of the hills, the forebears of the four clan blocs, sent their young to his host. Orcs held the forward lines at Dardan and died there in heaps, and when the battle was lost the masters who had promised them the Middle Lands left them on the field. The few who came home walked the whole way north through hostile country, and the Fire-Speakers still chant the Long Walk from Dardan at the Ember-Night, naming the hills where the walkers fell. From that walk came the two laws Goldoroth is built on. The first is the ring: a chief who cannot win his place with his own hands has no right to send others to die, so every chief, and since 4A 1452 every Warking, holds his seat only until a stronger challenger breaks him in the ring. The second is the moot's saying that no spirit rules the Dark, which the clans swore after Dardan and which many of them broke when they kept fighting in Volgan's name through the Second Age. The Fire-Mountain became holy later, when the clans moved into the volcano country and found that its heat kept off the cold and its smoke the glare of the sun; the Fire-Speakers say the mountain is the one master that never left them. In 4A 1748 the old grief divides the court: one party says Goldoroth must never march for a southern master again, and the other that this time the orcs should take the Middle Lands for themselves.

sign.device: The Crown of Broken Blades: a black iron crown of unequal jagged points, each one a broken sword-blade, on a fire-red field with a charcoal hem.
sign.origin: When Skarag of the Krumgul broke the last rival chief in the ring at Sungodor in 4A 1452, the chiefs of the four blocs brought him the blades of every chief he had beaten on his way to the ring, snapped at the hilt as the custom of the ring demands of the beaten. The chain-smiths of Sungodor hammered the broken blades into a ring for his head, and every Warking since has added the blade of the challenger he broke. The banner shows the crown as it first was, all jagged points and no gold, because the Volcano Clans hold that a crown of broken blades is the only crown an orc should trust.
sign.meaning: Goldoroth is made of beaten rivals: the banner promises the holds that every Warking won his seat with his own hands, and warns every chief that the crown has room for one more blade.

dynasties.name: The Warkings acclaimed at the Fire-Mountain
dynasties.notable: Not a family: each Warking is acclaimed by the moot of the four clan blocs and holds the throne until a stronger challenger breaks him in the ring. Skarag of the Krumgul was the first, and Warking Gorduth holds Cocanoor in 4A 1748.

events.name: The Long Walk from Dardan
events.summary: The orcs of the iron hills who had marched for Volgan were left on the field when Dardan was lost, and the few who lived walked home through hostile country; the Fire-Speakers chant the names of the hills where they fell at every Ember-Night.

events.name: The Moving of the Clans
events.summary: Orc clans began moving from the iron hills into the volcano country and the warm slopes of the Fire-Mountain, a migration that lasted three centuries.

events.name: The Acclamation at Sungodor
events.summary: Skarag of the Krumgul was acclaimed the first Warking, and the wars with Dondor began within the year.

events.name: The Iron Yoke
events.summary: The Warking made the gate-hold of the Dark Gate a tributary paying Cocanoor in iron, the first hold under the Iron Yoke.

events.name: The Reed Drowning
events.summary: A Goldoroth host sent to bring Dreson under the Yoke was led into the fens by the reed-council's guides and drowned; the warkingdom has not marched into the fens since.

events.name: The First Bombards
events.summary: The siege forges of Cocanoor cast their first bombards, fired with powder bought from the goblins of Burnikit, and broke Dondor's southern stockades.

rivalries.nature: The armed peace since 4A 1452: raids, beacon-fires and two wars over the border holds.
The host of the Free Moot of the holds that refuse the Iron Yoke.

countries.capitalReason: Cocanoor is the forge-city cut into black stone at the foot of the Fire-Mountain, where the volcano's heat and the iron of the arm meet; the Volcano Clans hold the mountain holy, and the Warking sits beneath it so that the Fire-Speakers stand at his side.
countries.today: Warking Gorduth rules some half a million orcs, with goblin quarters and a few trolls, from the forge-city below the Fire-Mountain. Goldoroth wants the whole Dark Lands and has not quite the strength to take them; its siege forges cast bombards with Burnikit's powder, its tribute holds pay in iron, and Volgan's envoys are received at court.

divergence.what: Goldoroth breaks the Accord and the Free Moot and unites the Dark Lands under the Warking.
divergence.consequence: One orc kingdom holds both arms of the Dark Lands and the straits on either side, and every crown of the North and the Middle Lands has a new great power on its doorstep.

divergence.what: The Warking swears to Volgan when he marches north.
divergence.consequence: The Dark Lands open a northern front for the Southern Dominion, and Goldoroth's fortunes are tied to Volgan's body.

divergence.what: The Dark Sea Accord breaks Goldoroth in the field.
divergence.consequence: The warkingdom falls back into four clan blocs fighting in the ring, and the free holds go back to answering to nobody.

divergence.what: The Fire-Speakers proclaim the vow of the Long Walk and the moot forbids any Warking to march for a southern master.
divergence.consequence: Goldoroth refuses Volgan whatever he offers, and the Accord faces a warkingdom that fights for the Dark Lands and for nothing beyond them.

countries.name: Dondor

founding.story: When Aenor's ships stopped coming to the Dondor plain around 1A 352, the garrison they left behind had married into the plain's few villages and could not go home. Its captains held a clan-moot on the forest edge and chose Dromand of the Barand, the strongest of them, as Brute-King, a title their orc neighbours gave them as an insult and they took as a boast. Their speech wore down over the centuries into Dondric, full of orc words, but they have kept their king and their iron.

roots.story: Dondor's men are the garrison that was never relieved. In the first half of the First Age Aen's heirs kept soldiers on the Dondor plain to hold the chart-harbours and watch the strait, men of the old Ainic crown who were paid in iron bars from Aenor's forges. When the ships stopped coming around 1A 352 the last pay-chest was opened on the stockade's ground and its bars divided among the hearths, one bar to each family, and the captains swore at the stockade to hold the plain as if the relief were still on its way. That chest is the root of the Hearth-Iron: every hearth of Dondor keeps a bar of iron and passes it to its eldest, and a house that loses its bar loses its place at the clan-moot. The captains chose the strongest of them, Dromand of the Barand, to lead, and the orcs called him Brute-King in scorn; his men kept the name as a boast and set the garrison's old helm on his head instead of a crown. Living beside the orc holds wore their speech into Dondric and their law into the blood-price, but it also taught them that orcs are neighbours and not one enemy, which is why Rovek of Dondor could lead Dark Lands soldiers into Edran's Grand Alliance, and why in 2A 1388 Brunmar of the Urdung took Dondor's spears south to close the Burning Gate of Nezer beside southern men and elves. In 4A 1748 Dondor still thinks of itself as the line that holds, and its beacon towers are the stockade's answer to Goldoroth's bombards.

sign.device: The Garrison Helm: an old open-faced iron helm with a tall ridge-crest, iron-grey on blood-red, with a black hem.
sign.origin: The Brute-Kings were never crowned. Dromand of the Barand was given the helm of the garrison's last captain, and every king since has been made by having that helm set on his head before the clan-moot. At Dardan the Charter of Free Banners let every people fight under its own sign, and Rovek of Dondor had none, so he lifted the king's helm on a spear above his veterans on the flank they held, and the helm on red cloth was sewn for the first time from that day's account. The spears of the Burning Gate hang around the same helm in the king's hall at Notbuton.
sign.meaning: We are the garrison that stayed: what Dondor holds it holds without relief, and the helm reminds every king that he is a captain of the line before he is a king.

dynasties.name: The Brute-Kings of the clan-moot
dynasties.notable: The clan-moot chooses each king from the strongest line of the moment; the Barand, the Gulung and the Urdung have each held the hall for centuries. King Dunmar of the Gulung reigns in 4A 1748.

events.name: The First Clan-Moot
events.summary: The garrison captains left on the Dondor plain chose Dromand of the Barand as their first Brute-King.

events.name: Rovek's Helm
events.summary: Under the Charter of Free Banners Rovek of Dondor raised the Brute-King's helm on a spear over his veterans at Dardan, and the helm on red became Dondor's banner.

events.name: The Burning Gate
events.summary: Dondor's spearmen under Brunmar of the Urdung marched south and stood with men of the southern kingdoms and an elven company to close the Burning Gate of Nezer; the clan-moot keeps their spears in the king's hall.

events.name: The Beacon Towers
events.summary: After Goldoroth's bombards broke the southern stockades, the Brute-King raised beacon towers on every hill of the plain so that the whole kingdom could be called to arms in a night.

events.name: The Dark Sea Accord
events.summary: Dondor and the sea orcs of Belonton swore the Accord on an iron bar and a skull sunk together in the Sea of Darkness.

events.name: The Dear Powder
events.summary: Dondor bought its first powder-pieces from Burnikit for the beacon towers, at a price the treasury still complains of.

countries.capitalReason: Notbuton stands on the forest edge of the Dondor plain facing the straits, where the old garrison's stockade stood; the plain feeds it, the forest hides it and the straits bring it Leren trade.
countries.today: King Dunmar rules about a quarter of a million men of the Dondor plain, the Dondor Forest, the lower Giant River and the fens from the Brute-King's hall. Dondor leads the Dark Sea Accord, keeps its beacon towers manned and a few dear powder-pieces in them, and needs the free holds' iron more than it likes to admit.

divergence.what: The Accord breaks when Belonton makes its own peace with Goldoroth.
divergence.consequence: Dondor stands alone against the warkingdom, and the Dondor plain becomes the Dark Lands' battlefield.

divergence.what: Dondor joins the free holds' Free Moot against the Iron Yoke.
divergence.consequence: Men and orcs stand together against Goldoroth for the first time since the Buried Wars, and the warkingdom is ringed.

divergence.what: Dondor sends the helm south again, as at the Burning Gate, to stand with the Middle Lands against the last war's hosts.
divergence.consequence: The Dark Lands are seen fighting on the side of the living once more, and Dondor earns friends beyond the straits at the price of leaving its own march thin.

countries.name: Dark Gate

founding.story: The pass at the foot of the Goldoroth Mountains is the only road from the Goldoroth arm to the south, and in 3A 880 an orc chief named Zugash built a gate-fort across it at Doldes and began taking a toll from every caravan that passed. His heirs tolled the road for six centuries as a free hold, until the first Warking of Goldoroth made them his tributary in 4A 1470.

roots.story: The pass at the foot of the Goldoroth Mountains has always been the throat of the Goldoroth arm, and the orcs who hold it remember every host that has gone through it. In the First Age Volgan's envoys came north by it and the orcs of the arm went south by it to the Southern Burning; after Dardan the broken bands came back through it, and those who kept the pass let them through for food and weapons, the first toll the pass ever took. In the Buried Wars the Necromancer's columns used the same road, and a band of free orcs held the narrows against them by stretching a smith's chain across the path at night, so that horses and carts broke on it in the dark. Zugash, who built the gate-fort at Doldes in 3A 880, was of that band, and he forged a great chain of three links to hang across the narrows and lowered it for any traveller who paid. From that chain comes the gate-hold's one law, that nothing and nobody passes unpaid and uncounted, not friends, not kin and not the envoys of a Great Spirit, and its tally-keepers still cut a notch for every caravan. When the first Warking made the gate-hold his tributary in 4A 1470 he did not take the chain down: he made the gate-chief pay Cocanoor out of it, so the chain that made Doldes free became the yoke it pays. In 4A 1748 the gate-chief tolls Volgan's envoys like any caravan, and remembers that the pass has been sold to the south before.

sign.device: The Gate-Chain: a heavy black chain of three great links hanging in an arc, on a dull gold field with a black hem.
sign.origin: The chain Zugash hung across the narrows at Doldes in 3A 880 still hangs there; each of its three links is the height of an orc, and it is lowered for every traveller who pays and for nobody who does not. Before it there was the smith's chain of the Buried Wars that broke the Necromancer's carts in the dark, and the gate-chiefs say the middle link was forged from it. The chain on gold was the toll-sign that caravans looked for on the road south, meaning that the gate was open to those who paid; since 4A 1470 the gate-chief has flown it under Cocanoor's banner.
sign.meaning: Nothing passes the gate unpaid and uncounted: to its own people the chain is their freedom, and to Goldoroth it is the yoke the gate-hold bears.

dynasties.name: The gate-chiefs of Doldes
dynasties.notable: Chiefs who hold the gate-fort until a stronger challenger breaks them in the ring; since 4A 1470 each new chief must be confirmed by the Warking.

events.name: The Smith's Chain
events.summary: Free orcs of the Goldoroth arm stretched a smith's chain across the narrows of the pass by night, and the Necromancer's carts and horses broke on it in the dark; the band that did it held the pass from then on.

events.name: The Gate-Fort
events.summary: Zugash built the gate-fort across the pass and began the toll.

events.name: The Iron Yoke
events.summary: The gate-hold became Goldoroth's first tributary, paying Cocanoor in iron from its tolls.

events.name: The Southern Envoys
events.summary: Envoys from Volgan's Southern Dominion came north through the pass for the first time in the age, and the gate-chief tolled them like any caravan.

countries.capitalReason: Doldes is the gate-fort built across the narrowest point of the Dark Gate pass, where no caravan can go round it.
countries.today: About forty thousand orcs hold the pass and Bold's border under a gate-chief confirmed by the Warking. Every caravan pays the toll, and Volgan's envoys pass through it to every court of the Dark Lands.

divergence.what: The gate-chief throws off the Iron Yoke.
divergence.consequence: Goldoroth loses its road south and the toll's iron, and the Free Moot gains a hold at the warkingdom's back door.

divergence.what: The gate-chief opens the pass to a southern host.
divergence.consequence: Volgan's armies can come north through the Goldoroth arm, and the Dark Lands are a front of the last war.

divergence.what: The gate-chief keeps the chain raised against everyone, Cocanoor's tribute-takers and Volgan's envoys alike.
divergence.consequence: The Goldoroth arm is cut from the south in both directions, Volgan's envoys must come by sea, and the Warking must take the gate by force or lose its iron.

countries.name: Burnikit

founding.story: The goblin warrens under the Goldoroth Mountains had opened their deep ways to the Necromancer's hosts and regretted it, and in 3A 1004, when his recruiters came again, the warrens chose their loudest and cleverest boss, a goblin called Snikkit, as the first Big Snik, so that one voice would lie to the recruiters for all of them. The trick worked, and the warrens have kept a Big Snik and their freedom ever since, owing nothing to any hobgoblin king.

roots.story: The goblins of the warm caves under the Goldoroth Mountains were there before any orc warking, living in the deepest and warmest rock because they hate the cold and the sun weakens them. They have one great grief and one great trick, and both made Burnikit what it is. The grief is the Unpaid: in 2A 2110 the warrens opened their deep ways to the Necromancer's hosts for a promised price, his recruiters took goblins with them as guides and levies, and neither the price nor the goblins came back. The warrens cut a notch on the Unpaid Stick for every goblin lost, and it hangs in the hall of fire still. The trick is the Fire at the Door: when the recruiters came again in 3A 1004, the warrens chose their loudest and cleverest boss, Snikkit, to speak for all of them, and Snikkit had a fire of the yellow crusts lit in the mouth of every deep way and told the recruiters that the warrens were burning with a sickness; the stinking smoke made the lie true enough to send them away. The fire in the hall's mouth was never let out, and it is the great lamp of Burnikzig. From the grief comes the warrens' law that payment comes first and nobody is trusted on credit; from the trick come the Big Sniks, one voice that lies for everyone, and the craft of the yellow crusts, which in 4A 1566 became the first powder of the Dark Lands. Burnikit sells to whoever pays and charges its enemies more, because it learned from the Necromancer what a promise is worth.

sign.device: The Fire at the Door: a black tunnel-arch with a yellow fire burning in its mouth, on a rust-red field with a yellow hem.
sign.origin: The sign is Snikkit's lie of 3A 1004: the mouth of a deep way with the sulphur fire burning in it, the sight that sent the Necromancer's recruiters back up the mountain. The goblins painted it at the mouth of every warren afterwards as a warning to strangers, and when Burnikit began to sell its powder in 4A 1566 the same sign was burned into every keg, so that the orcs of Cocanoor and the men of Notbuton learned to read it before they could read anything else of the warrens.
sign.meaning: Keep out unless you pay: what burns inside is the warrens' own, it was paid for once in goblins, and it costs every buyer dear.

dynasties.name: The Big Sniks of Burnikzig
dynasties.notable: Each Big Snik is the loudest and cleverest boss the warrens will follow; the present Big Snik is called Skritix.

events.name: The Deep Ways Opened
events.summary: The warrens opened their tunnels to the Necromancer's hosts and closed them again when he did not pay.

events.name: The Great Lamp
events.summary: The warrens chose their first Big Snik to keep the Necromancer's recruiters out, and lit the great lamp in the hall of fire that has not gone out since.

events.name: The Fire at the Door
events.summary: Snikkit, the first Big Snik, had sulphur fires lit in the mouth of every deep way and told the Necromancer's recruiters that the warrens were burning with sickness; the smoke sent them away, and the fire in the hall's mouth became the great lamp.

events.name: The Fire-Powder
events.summary: The goblins learned to make a burning powder from the volcano's yellow crusts and the saltpetre of their caves, the first powder of the Dark Lands, and began selling it to the highest bidder.

events.name: Powder for Both
events.summary: Burnikit sold powder to Goldoroth's siege forges and powder-pieces to Dondor's beacon towers in the same year, and charged Dondor more.

countries.capitalReason: Burnikzig, the hall of fire, lies in the warmest caves under the Goldoroth Mountains, heated by the volcano, where goblins who hate the sun and the cold can live all year.
countries.today: About sixty thousand goblins, with a few hobgoblins as guards and haulers of stone, live in the warm deep caves under a Big Snik. They are the best powder-makers of the region and sell to whoever pays most, which in 4A 1748 is usually Goldoroth.

divergence.what: The Accord buys Burnikit's favour and the Big Snik stops selling to Cocanoor.
divergence.consequence: Goldoroth's bombards fall silent for want of powder, and the warkingdom's siege forges must find another supplier.

divergence.what: The Big Snik sells powder to every side in the last war.
divergence.consequence: Every Dark Lands host goes to war with fire, and Burnikit grows rich on all of them.

divergence.what: A power pays the Unpaid in full, gold for every notch on the stick, before it asks Burnikit for anything.
divergence.consequence: The Big Snik gives that power the only true promise the warrens have ever given: powder for it alone, and the deep ways shut to its enemies.

countries.name: Veshazel

founding.story: The black south of the Goldoroth arm, where ash covers everything and nothing grows, was empty of everything but devils' roosts until demons came up out of the south and raised a hall of ash at Ozmath-Vesh in 4A 1180, under a lord who keeps a pact-name that only his pact knows. Men and orcs who had nowhere else to go came to serve the hall as thralls, and the lordship has belonged to no master since.

roots.story: The demons of the hall of ash are not Volgan's, and they are no longer the King of Demons'. The elves call demons corrupted angels; the thralls of Ozmath-Vesh know only that their masters came up out of the south. The hall's own telling, which it gives its thralls in pieces, is that its lord was once of a house of the Nether's court, one of the houses that compete for the king's favour and the right to open portals, and that in the Third Age, when the portals were closing one by one as the houses quarrelled with Elzon's order, his house lost that right and its standing. Rather than serve a rival house, the lord took the house's pact-name out of the court with him, which the court counts as theft, and walked north with the few demons who held to him, by vents and black shores that nobody has charted, until in 4A 1180 he came to the Goldoroth Ash Fields, where only devils roosted. He raked the black rock with his claws to mark the bounds of his lordship and raised a hall of pressed ash inside them. Everything the hall does comes from that break. It swears to no master, because a house that serves loses its name; it binds its thralls by the pact-rite of blood and ash and marks them with the lord's three scores, because a lordship of a few hundred demons must hold its mortals fast; and it fears the court it left as much as the court resents it. The thralls, broken orcs and debtor men who came after 4A 1390, keep a custom of their own: a thrall who has served seven winters may ask the lord for a name. In 4A 1748 the lordship is courted by the Southern Dominion, which it refused in 4A 1650, and watched from the Nether.

sign.device: The Three Scores: three red claw-scores raked slantwise across an ash-grey field, with a black hem.
sign.origin: When the lord came to the Ash Fields in 4A 1180 he marked the bounds of his lordship by raking the black rock with his claws, three scores at every corner, and the scores are still there, glowing faintly in the dark of the year. Every thrall who swears to the hall is marked on the arm with the same three scores, and every pact the hall makes is sealed with them in ash. The thralls sewed the scores on grey cloth when they first marched in the hall's service, having no other sign, and the lord let it stand because it names what the hall is: a bound marked out of nothing by one who would not kneel.
sign.meaning: What is marked belongs to the hall: to its thralls the scores promise a master who keeps his own word and nobody else's, and to everyone else they warn that the hall's bargains are never paid in gold.

dynasties.name: The pact-lords of the hall of ash
dynasties.notable: Lords of two-beat names and hidden pact-names; the present lord is called Thazael at the courts of others. The lordship is sworn to neither Volgan nor Goldoroth.

events.name: The Hall of Ash
events.summary: Demons raised the hall of ash at Ozmath-Vesh on the Goldoroth Ash Fields.

events.name: The Bounds Raked
events.summary: The lord of the hall marked the bounds of his lordship on the Ash Fields with three claw-scores at every corner, and every thrall and pact of the hall has carried the same mark since.

events.name: The Thralls of the Ash
events.summary: Orcs broken in the clan wars of the volcano country and men fleeing debts on the coasts came to the Ash Fields and swore to the hall, and the lordship has had more mortal subjects than demons since.

events.name: The Dominion's Envoys
events.summary: When the Southern Dominion was sworn to Volgan, its envoys came to Ozmath-Vesh and asked the lord to swear too; he sent them home with gifts and without his oath.

rivalries.nature: The warkingdom wants the Ash Fields' shore and fears what lives on them.

countries.capitalReason: Ozmath-Vesh, the hall of ash, stands on the black shore facing the Sea of Dolon, the one place on the Goldoroth arm that nobody else wanted and the shore that leads south toward the Ember Lands.
countries.today: About two thousand souls live on the Goldoroth Ash Fields: a few hundred demons and their mortal thralls under a lord who keeps a pact-name. The lordship is shunned by its neighbours and courted by the Southern Dominion, which wants it as its northern foothold.

divergence.what: The lord swears to the Southern Dominion when Volgan marches.
divergence.consequence: The Dominion has a foothold on the Dark Lands' southern shore, and Goldoroth has demons at its back.

divergence.what: The lord lends fire and terror to one Dark Lands power for a price.
divergence.consequence: That power fights with demons beside it, and the price is named in the pact, not in gold.

divergence.what: A house of the Nether's court comes north to take back the pact-name the lord carried away.
divergence.consequence: Demons fight demons on the Ash Fields, the thralls must choose a master, and Goldoroth's southern shore burns whichever house wins.

countries.name: Blackton

founding.story: The harbour towns at the end of the Iron Road had been Dondric fishing villages until Leren merchants began to settle at Dontadur in 4A 1071 to buy Dondor's iron, and within a generation the five harbours were walled towns of mixed Dondric and Leren folk who wanted no king. In 4A 1102 they swore a league of five towns under a town moot, and they have defended their walls and their trade together since.

roots.story: The five walled harbours of the eastern coast grew on a shore where two old enemies met. In the Raiding Years of the Second Age the beaches below the Iron Road were the launching places of the iron holds' raids across the Northern Dark Strait, and Leren fleets came back to burn them so often that the Dondric fishers who lived there learned to build in stone and to keep no lord who could be blamed. When Leren merchants came to Dontadur in 4A 1071 to buy Dondor's iron, they came as the grandchildren of those who had burned the beaches, and they married the grandchildren of those who had raided the North. The league sworn in 4A 1102 was made to keep that peace: the five towns gave their harbour-keys to one moot, and the founders set up a high seat in the moot-hall at Dontadur and swore that nobody would ever sit in it, so that no Dondric house and no Leren house could rule the other. The empty seat is why Blackton chooses a moot-speaker each year who sits below it, why its burghers hold that a town is free when it has walls and no master, and why the charter quarrel of 4A 1688 was so bitter: a Leren-born burgher asked to sit in the seat, and the moot refused him by a single voice. In 4A 1748 every generation argues about the seat again, and the towns trade with everyone while keeping out of the Accord's wars where they can.

sign.device: The Empty Seat: a tall-backed high seat, empty, in white on black, with a sea-green hem.
sign.origin: The seat stands in the moot-hall at Dontadur where the founders set it in 4A 1102: a high seat of black-stained timber with a tall back, built for a lord and sworn to stay empty. At every moot the speaker turns to it before the vote and says that the seat is still empty, and the burghers answer that it will stay so. The towns sewed the empty seat on their banners when they first manned their walls together, white on black because the seat is black and the cloth was the burghers' mourning colour, and the Leren quarter keeps an old copy of that banner from the charter quarrel.
sign.meaning: No master in Blackton: the five towns rule themselves together, and the empty seat warns every would-be lord, Leren or Dondric, that the towns mean to keep it empty.

dynasties.name: The town moot of the five harbours
dynasties.notable: Each walled town sends its burghers to the moot at Dontadur, which chooses a moot-speaker each year; whether to keep the moot or take a lord's charter is argued in every generation.

events.name: The Leren Landing
events.summary: Leren merchants settled at Dontadur to buy the iron of the Iron Road, and their ships have come every season since.

events.name: The League of Five Towns
events.summary: The five walled harbours swore their league under a town moot.

events.name: The Empty Seat
events.summary: The founders of the league set up a high seat in the moot-hall at Dontadur and swore that nobody would sit in it, so that no Dondric or Leren house could rule the five towns.

events.name: The Charter Quarrel
events.summary: A Leren-born burgher offered to rule the league as lord under a charter; the moot refused by a single voice, and the quarrel still divides the towns.

countries.capitalReason: Dontadur is the largest of the five walled harbours, where the Iron Road from the Dondor hills meets the sea and the Leren ships moor.
countries.today: About two hundred thousand people of mixed Dondric and Leren blood live in the five walled harbour towns of the eastern coast. Blackton sells Dondor's iron to the North, keeps out of the Accord's wars where it can, and argues about its charter.

divergence.what: The moot takes a lord's charter under a Leren-born lord.
divergence.consequence: Blackton leans to Lerendor, and the Dark Shore gains a friend of the High Crown.

divergence.what: The five towns join the Dark Sea Accord.
divergence.consequence: Dondor gains harbours and ships, and Goldoroth gains another enemy on the coast.

divergence.what: A burgher, a Leren lord or a Dondric king's son sits in the empty seat.
divergence.consequence: Blackton becomes a lordship, the towns that swore against it rise or leave the league, and the coast's neighbours each back their own claimant to the seat.

countries.name: Belonton

founding.story: The sea orcs of the Belonton borderlands and isles were raiders of the straits for the whole Third Age, and in 3A 940 their holds swore a confederacy at the harbour of Notle so that their ships would raid others rather than each other. The Sea-Chief is chosen by the voyages he has won, and the confederacy has kept the Salt Tithe and its ships ever since.

roots.story: The sea orcs say they were rowers before they were raiders. In the second millennium of the First Age Volgan's eastern and southern clients crossed the waters toward the Middle Lands in great galleys, and the oars of many were pulled by orcs chained to the benches, bought or taken from the holds of the Dark Lands. When Dardan was lost the masters fled south and left a fleet of galleys stranded in the Belonton waters with their rowers still chained; the rowers broke their shackles, threw the last overseers into the sea and took the Lestern Isles and the borderland coast with the masters' own ships. They have been a seafaring people ever since, as no other orcs are. From the benches they kept three things. The Salt Tithe: every voyage gives the sea a measure of salt, the share the masters used to take from them, now paid to the sea alone. The Sea-Chief chosen by voyages won, because on the benches only the stroke counted and nobody's birth. And the oath that no sea orc rows for a master again, which is why Belonton raided every strait through the Third Age and swore its confederacy at Notle in 3A 940 only so that its ships would raid others rather than each other. It is also why the Dark Sea Accord of 4A 1604 holds: the sea orcs and the men of Dondor are both peoples left behind by masters who never came back for them, and the Accord's iron bar and skull were sunk together as the bench-chains had been. In 4A 1748 Goldoroth offers Belonton harbours and plunder, and the Sea-Chiefs hear in the offer the sound of a bench.

sign.device: The Broken Shackle: an open iron shackle snapped through at one side, salt-white on deep sea-green, with a black hem.
sign.origin: The shackle is the rowers' own. When the bench-chains were broken in the Belonton waters after Dardan, each rower kept the shackle from his own ankle, and the oldest holds of the confederacy still keep a few of them, eaten thin by salt, in their halls. When the holds swore at Notle in 3A 940 each captain threw one shackle into the harbour and the Sea-Chief nailed the last to his mast, and Belonton's ships have flown a broken shackle on green ever since; Leren sailors call it the bench-mark and know it before they see the hull.
sign.meaning: No sea orc rows for a master again: to friends the shackle promises a free people of the sea, and to Goldoroth it says that Belonton remembers what masters cost.

dynasties.name: The Sea-Chiefs of Notle
dynasties.notable: Chosen by the holds for the voyages they have won; the present Sea-Chief is Rukhag of the Ghashak, who won his chair by bringing home a Leren ship whole.

events.name: The Breaking of the Benches
events.summary: Orc rowers chained to the benches of Volgan's clients' galleys were left stranded in the Belonton waters after Dardan; they broke their shackles, drowned their overseers and took the isles and the coast with the masters' ships.

events.name: The Confederacy at Notle
events.summary: The sea-orc holds swore their confederacy and chose their first Sea-Chief.

events.name: The Burning of Nuadoso
events.summary: Belonton's ships burned the shared seat of the North's double crown of Keredor-Hellekton, and the next year Lerendor's fleet burned Notle in return.

events.name: The Dark Sea Accord
events.summary: Belonton swore the Accord with Dondor on an iron bar and a skull sunk together in the Sea of Darkness.

rivalries.nature: The warkingdom that wants the sea orcs' harbours.
The fleet that burned Notle in 4A 1532.

countries.capitalReason: Notle is the sea orcs' harbour on the borderland coast, sheltered by the Lestern Isles, from which Belonton's ships can reach every strait of the Dark Lands.
countries.today: About eighty thousand sea orcs live on the Belonton borderlands, the Gull Kingdom's cliffs and the Lestern Isles. They are Dondor's partner in the Accord, keep the Salt Tithe and raid only those the Accord does not protect.

divergence.what: The Sea-Chief makes a separate peace with Goldoroth.
divergence.consequence: The Accord breaks, and Dondor faces the warkingdom with no fleet beside it.

divergence.what: Belonton's ships guard the Northern Dark Strait in the last war.
divergence.consequence: The dead and the living alike find the strait watched by sea orcs, and the North owes Belonton a debt it never expected.

divergence.what: Volgan's admirals offer the Sea-Chief galleys, pay and the Middle Lands' coasts if Belonton rows for the Southern Dominion.
divergence.consequence: Holds that take the offer break the bench-oath, the confederacy splits between those who row and those who burn the offer, and the Accord loses half a fleet in a season.

countries.name: Bordon

founding.story: In the Buried Wars the gorge of the Black Road by Soun Lake was the free holds' road between the iron hills, and in 3A 700 an orc chief named Kargesk took it from the Necromancer's garrison and built a hold at Zubudor to keep it. When the wars ended his heirs turned the hold's barracks into caravan inns, and Bordon has lived by the road ever since.

roots.story: The Black Road through the gorge by Soun Lake is the oldest road of the iron hills, worn by orc carriers long before Aen and blackened by the slag they spread to keep it firm in the wet. In the Buried Wars it was the free holds' only road between the hills, and the Necromancer's garrison sat in the gorge to close it. In 3A 700 Kargesk of the road-clans brought the free runners through the gorge at night by blowing a great horn from the cliff-top at the moment the garrison changed its watch, so that every runner on the road moved at once and the garrison fought shadows; by dawn the runners held the gorge and the garrison was dead or gone. Kargesk built the hold at Zubudor where his horn had sounded, and the horn hangs in its gate. When the wars ended his heirs turned the barracks into caravan inns, and the horn became the sign of the Road-Peace: when a caravan enters the gorge the horn is blown, and from that note until the caravan leaves no blade may be drawn on it, by the hold or by anyone else, on pain of the ring. Bordon lives by that peace. It is why caravans pay its tolls gladly, why its chiefs take Volgan's gifts and Goldoroth's threats with the same grin, and why the Night of the Trolls of 4A 1390 became Bordon's own grief: the caravan the troll king smashed had camped in the forest beyond the horn's reach and was under no peace, because it had left the road. In 4A 1748 the hold keeps the road open to everyone, and every master who wants the Black Road must first want the Road-Peace broken.

sign.device: Kargesk's Horn: a great curved black war-horn bound with two red bands, on a dust-ochre field with a red hem.
sign.origin: The horn Kargesk blew from the gorge's cliff in 3A 700 hangs in Zubudor's gate, a great curved horn of black bone bound with red-painted iron bands, too heavy for one orc to lift to his mouth. It is blown for every caravan that enters the Road-Peace and for every challenge of the ring. Bordon's road-wardens carry the horn sewn on ochre cloth, the colour of the gorge's dust, so that a caravan master can tell from a distance that the riders coming toward him are the road's keepers and not raiders.
sign.meaning: While the horn's note lasts the road is at peace: the horn promises safe passage to every caravan and warns every army that Bordon's road is not for sale.

dynasties.name: The road-chiefs of Zubudor
dynasties.notable: Chiefs who keep the iron and the ring until they are challenged; the present chief's line has held the hold for three challenges running.

events.name: The Road Taken
events.summary: Kargesk took the Black Road gorge from the Necromancer's garrison and built the hold at Zubudor.

events.name: The Caravan Inns
events.summary: The hold's barracks became caravan inns, and Bordon began to live by the road rather than the sword.

events.name: The Road-Peace
events.summary: When the barracks became caravan inns, Kargesk's horn was given to the road: it is blown when a caravan enters the gorge, and no blade may be drawn on that caravan until it leaves.

events.name: The Night of the Trolls
events.summary: A caravan camped in the Troll Forest beside the Black Road was smashed in the night by the troll king, and Bordon's chiefs have forbidden caravans to camp there since.

rivalries.nature: The warkingdom wants the Black Road under the Iron Yoke.

countries.capitalReason: Zubudor is the hold in the Black Road's gorge by Soun Lake, the narrowest point of the road between the iron hills, where caravans must stop.
countries.today: About fifty thousand orcs of the Iron Clans keep the Black Road and its caravan inns. Bordon is a separate hold that belongs to nobody, takes Volgan's gifts and Goldoroth's threats with the same grin, and knows exactly where the Troll Forest begins.

divergence.what: Bordon bows to the Iron Yoke.
divergence.consequence: Goldoroth controls the Black Road, and the free holds' iron goes to Cocanoor.

divergence.what: Bordon holds the Free Moot together when Goldoroth presses.
divergence.consequence: The free holds keep their road, and the warkingdom must fight for every hill.

divergence.what: A great power's soldiers draw blades on a caravan inside the Road-Peace.
divergence.consequence: The caravans leave the Black Road, the free holds' iron stops moving, and Bordon goes to war with that power under the horn, with every hold that uses the road beside it.

countries.name: Dreson

founding.story: In the Buried Wars orcs who would not fight for the Necromancer fled into the fens his garrisons could not cross, and in 3A 520 they built a hall on black piles in the reeds at Dolido and chose a reed-council to rule them. The fens have kept Dreson free ever since; its folk live on eels, peat and bog-iron, and armies that come after them do not come back.

roots.story: The fen orcs of Dreson are the levies who would not go. In the Buried Wars the Necromancer's recruiters took the young orcs of the iron holds in chains for his garrisons in Aenor, and in 3A 520 a column of them broke their chains on the march and fled into the fens, where the garrisons' horses sank and their carts could not follow. Three of them, who had grown up as eel-fishers on the fen's edge, knew the paths, and they drove the first three piles into the reeds at Dolido so that the others had somewhere to stand. Those three were the first path-elders, and the reed-council of Dreson is their heirs: elders who know the fen paths and teach them only by walking them, never by drawing them, so that no map of the fens exists outside the council's memory. From the flight comes the fen-law that no chains enter the fens: no slave, no thrall and no prisoner is held at Dolido, and an escaped captive who reaches the reeds is free. From the paths comes Dreson's way of war, the guide who walks ahead of a host and then is no longer there, which drowned the Necromancer's patrols in the Third Age and a Goldoroth host in the Reed Drowning of 4A 1561. The hall on black piles still stands on the first three piles, and every path-elder is buried standing in the reeds beside them. In 4A 1748 Dreson belongs to nobody, and the reed-council weighs every envoy against the fen-law.

sign.device: The Three Piles: three black piles standing upright, the middle one tallest, rising out of a wavy band of fen-green, on a pale reed-yellow field.
sign.origin: The three piles are the first ones driven at Dolido in 3A 520 by the three eel-fishers who led the escaped levies into the fens, and the hall on black piles still stands on them. The reed-council keeps three path-elders in their memory, and when a council is called its elders touch the three piles before they sit. The fen orcs embroidered the piles on reed-coloured cloth when the Free Moot first asked them to send a band to the hills, so that the other holds would know the fen-folk by their own sign and never mistake them for anybody's levies.
sign.meaning: We stand where no one else can: the piles promise refuge to every runaway and warn every host that the ground beneath Dreson belongs to the council alone.

dynasties.name: The reed-council of Dolido
dynasties.notable: Elders who know the fen paths sit in the hall on black piles; the council chooses a chief to keep the iron and the ring, and can unmake him.

events.name: The Hall on Black Piles
events.summary: Orcs fleeing the Necromancer's levies built the hall at Dolido and chose the first reed-council.

events.name: The Broken Column
events.summary: A column of young orcs taken in chains for the Necromancer's garrisons broke its chains on the march and fled into the fens, where three eel-fishers among them knew the paths.

events.name: The Buried Wars
events.summary: The fen orcs struck the Necromancer's garrisons from the reeds and vanished into them, and the Order never brought them under its yoke.

events.name: The Reed Drowning
events.summary: The reed-council's guides led a Goldoroth host into the deep fens and left it there.

rivalries.nature: The host drowned in the fens in 4A 1561 is not forgotten in Cocanoor.

countries.capitalReason: Dolido is the hall on black piles in the middle of the fens, reached only by paths the reed-council knows, which is why it was built there.
countries.today: About forty thousand orcs live in the fens on eels, peat and bog-iron under the reed-council. Dreson is a separate hold that belongs to nobody, and its fens swallow armies.

divergence.what: The reed-council guides another power's host through the fens.
divergence.consequence: An army can cross the Dark Lands where nobody expects one, and Dreson's neutrality is spent.

divergence.what: The fens take in the free holds' folk when Goldoroth marches.
divergence.consequence: The Free Moot cannot be destroyed while the fens hold, and the warkingdom's victory is never complete.

divergence.what: The thralls of Veshazel and the captives of Goldoroth's raids learn that the fen-law frees anyone who reaches the reeds, and run to Dreson in numbers.
divergence.consequence: Dreson grows with runaways and becomes the refuge of the Dark Lands, and both the hall of ash and the warkingdom come to the fens' edge to take back what they call theirs.

countries.name: Dulundur

founding.story: The four valleys of the long valley were four quarrelling holds until, late in the Third Age, the Necromancer's last levies came for their young orcs. In 3A 1150 the four chiefs lit four fires in one hall at Lesderle and swore to keep them burning together, and the Four Fires have ruled the long valley since, each valley keeping its own chief and its own fire.

roots.story: The four valleys of the long valley were four holds of the Iron Clans long before Aen, each with its own fire-rite: the north valley kept its fire in an iron basket, the river valley on a flat stone, the high valley in a pit and the south valley on an open hearth, and each held the others' rites in contempt. What made one realm of them was the Necromancer's last levy. In the late Third Age his recruiters came for the young orcs of all four valleys in the same season, and each valley found that it could not hide its young alone. In 3A 1150 the four chiefs carried their fires to the hall at Lesderle, the only hall all four could reach in a day, lit them side by side on one hearthstone and swore that the four fires would burn together or not at all; the recruiters found four valleys under arms and went back without a single orc. From that oath come Dulundur's laws: each valley keeps its own chief and its own fire, the hall speaks only when all four agree, and an envoy who asks one valley to break from the others is put out of the hall, as Goldoroth's envoy was in 4A 1612. The goblins of the valleys, who ran messages between the fires on the night of the oath, keep a lamp beside them in the hall to this day. From the same oath came the Free Moot of 4A 1488, when the Four Fires called the free holds to Lesderle against the Iron Yoke and offered them the same bargain: keep your own fire, and keep it beside ours. In 4A 1748 Dulundur is the free holds' strongest voice, and its people say that a hall with one fire is a hall waiting for a master.

sign.device: The Four Fires: four red flames rising side by side from one black hearthstone, their tips leaning together, on charcoal with a yellow hem.
sign.origin: The four fires lit on one hearthstone at Lesderle in 3A 1150 have burned there ever since, each tended by its own valley's keepers. When the four valleys first marched together under the oath their chiefs had no common sign, and the hall's weavers stitched the four fires on one stone so that every valley could see its own fire in the banner and none of them stood above the others. The holds of the Free Moot carry small copies of it to Lesderle when they come to speak.
sign.meaning: Four fires, one hall: no valley stands alone and none rules the others, and the banner warns Cocanoor that an iron yoke must put out all four fires at once.

dynasties.name: The Four Fires of Lesderle
dynasties.notable: Four chiefs, one for each valley, each holding his fire until challenged; the hall chooses one to speak for the long valley at the Free Moot. Its goblin quarters keep a lamp beside the fires.

events.name: The Four Fires Lit
events.summary: The four valley chiefs lit their fires in one hall at Lesderle and swore to keep them together.

events.name: The Free Moot
events.summary: When Goldoroth's Iron Yoke took the Dark Gate, the Four Fires called the free holds to Lesderle, and the Free Moot has settled tolls and iron prices there since.

events.name: The Fire Kept
events.summary: Goldoroth's envoys offered the Four Fires a place under the Yoke for one valley; the hall put out that valley's envoy instead of its fire.

rivalries.nature: The Free Moot stands against the Iron Yoke.

countries.capitalReason: Lesderle is the moot hold in the largest of the four valleys, where the four valley roads meet; the Four Fires burn in its hall because it is the only hall all four chiefs could reach in a day.
countries.today: About a hundred and fifty thousand orcs, with goblin quarters, live in the long valley's four holds under the Four Fires. Dulundur hosts the Free Moot against the Iron Yoke and is the free holds' strongest voice.

divergence.what: The Free Moot holds together under Dulundur's lead when Goldoroth presses.
divergence.consequence: The warkingdom faces a league of holds rather than a row of single ones, and the Dark Lands stay divided.

divergence.what: One of the Four Fires goes out when a valley bows to Goldoroth.
divergence.consequence: The long valley is divided, the Free Moot loses its hall, and the Iron Yoke reaches the iron hills.

divergence.what: The Four Fires carry a fire from the hearthstone to every hold of the Free Moot, and each hold lights it beside its own.
divergence.consequence: The Free Moot becomes one hall of many fires, a realm of free holds that Goldoroth must fight as a whole, and that no single chief can sell.

countries.name: Troll Forest

founding.story: Trolls have lived in the forest beside the Black Road for as long as any orc remembers, and they call it Grootoom, the great forest-place. Men and orcs date the realm from 4A 1390, the first time Bordon's caravan masters wrote down that a king of the trolls walked out at night and smashed a camp, and they have written down every such night since. The trolls live with their king in the great cave of Holos and keep the old rule that the oldest unbeaten troll leads each group.

roots.story: The trolls of Grootoom remember nothing written and forget nothing told. They have lived in the forest beside the Black Road for as long as any orc remembers, and their oldest telling is the King-Stones. A troll who is caught by the sun turns slowly to stone, and the trolls hold that a troll king who has grown too great and too old does not die in the cave: he walks out of Holos at the end of a night and stands at the forest's edge facing the dawn, and the sun makes him a stone that keeps watch for ever. The forest's edge is ringed with these hunched grey stones, and the trolls name each one and bring it silver and bones; this is the Hunger and the Stone that men have heard of, and the reason no troll lets anyone cut the forest's edge. From the King-Stones come the forest's laws: the oldest unbeaten troll leads each group, because one day he will be a stone and must have earned it; the forest's bounds are where the kings stand, and nobody enters them; and silver, which the trolls say is cold like stone, belongs to the kings, which is why realms that pay the troll silver are let through and why the king smashes a camp that crosses the stones without paying. The present king, Smash, is by far the largest troll and walks only at night, because the sun has already begun to turn him; his trolls say his stone will be the greatest on the edge. In 4A 1748 the forest belongs to nobody, and every power that wants the Black Road must reckon with kings who have watched it for longer than its road-chiefs have kept it.

sign.device: The King-Stone: a hunched grey standing stone in the shape of a crouching troll, on deep forest-green, with a dark silver hem.
sign.origin: The King-Stones stand at the forest's edge, each in the shape of a troll crouched to face the dawn, and the trolls bring them silver. When the trolls march, they carry before them a great slab of hide daubed in ash and silver with the shape of a King-Stone, the only standard trolls have ever made, so that the kings go with them. Bordon's caravan masters drew the same shape in their record of the Night of the Trolls in 4A 1390, and the Dondor envoy who left the first troll silver in 4A 1515 laid it at the foot of a King-Stone.
sign.meaning: The kings are watching: the stone promises the trolls that their bounds are kept for ever, and warns every intruder that the forest's dead kings are its walls.

dynasties.name: The troll kings of Holos
dynasties.notable: The forest's king is by far the largest troll and rules the trolls of this forest only; the present king is called Smash, and he walks at night because sunlight slowly turns him to stone.

events.name: The Night of the Trolls
events.summary: A caravan camped in the forest beside the Black Road was smashed by the troll king in the night, and Bordon's caravan masters began to keep a record of his nights.

events.name: The Troll Silver
events.summary: A Dondor envoy left silver at the forest's edge and was let through unharmed; since then realms that want to cross pay the troll silver.

events.name: The Burned Edge
events.summary: Goldoroth's raiders tried to burn the forest's edge to make a road; Smash came out of Holos that night and the raiders' camp was not found until spring.

countries.capitalReason: Holos is the great cave in the forest's heart where the troll king lives with the trolls who guard him, out of the sun that turns trolls to stone.
countries.today: About six hundred forest trolls live in the Troll Forest under Smash, king of these trolls and no others. The forest belongs to nobody; realms that pay the troll silver are left alone, and armies that camp there are smashed by night.

divergence.what: An invader burns or fells the forest.
divergence.consequence: Smash wakes the whole forest against the invader, and every army near the Black Road suffers his nights.

divergence.what: A realm pays the troll silver faithfully through the last war.
divergence.consequence: That realm may cross the forest unharmed, and the Black Road becomes its road.

divergence.what: Smash walks out of Holos into the dawn during the last war and becomes the greatest stone on the forest's edge.
divergence.consequence: A younger king leads the trolls, the bounds are kept more fiercely than ever, and every realm that paid Smash must pay his heir again.

countries.name: Hoorunoron

founding.story: The giants of the low hills behind the cairn-line, at the Giant Forest's edge, were there before the orcs came to the iron hills, and men and orcs have always known that the line of cairns below the Dark Forests is not to be crossed. They date the giants' realm from 4A 1210, when a band of Dondor woodcutters crossed the cairn-line and the giants came out of the forest and carried them back over it, one under each arm, and set them down without a word.

roots.story: The giants of Hoorunoron are the Forgotten Giants, the giants of the low hills of the drowned Low Country, and they carried their line with them. Long before Aen they lived on the low hills of the Low Country as partners of the cord-mothers' moot, raising the long sea-dikes from field-stone and keeping their cairn-fields on the high ground. Their cairn-keepers warned the Moot that the land was being asked for too much, and when the mothers drew harder and the Night of the Sea broke the last dikes, the giants did not go down with the land. They withdrew north-east, taking with them the stones of the broken dikes, carried one under each arm, and raised them again as the line of cairns below the Dark Forests that men call the Borderline of Giants. The line is a dike rebuilt on dry land, and that is why it may not be crossed: a breached dike lets in what drowns everything, and the giants will not see a line of theirs broken twice. From the same night they keep their own count, and the oldest stones of the count, laid in the first years after the sea came, lie at the head of the line by the Giant River, where a succession of keepers has added to them. They say of the Low Country only that the land was asked for too much, and nothing of what lies under the sea. The forest beside their hills holds giants of another people, of whom the Forgotten Giants say nothing at all. Men and orcs date Hoorunoron from 4A 1210, when Dondor woodcutters who crossed the line were carried back over it; the giants date it from the night the sea came.

sign.device: The Dike-Cairn: a tall cairn of stacked grey stones standing on a wavy blue-black band, on moss-green, with a stone-grey hem.
sign.origin: Every cairn of the Borderline is built of stones from the broken sea-dikes of the drowned Low Country, carried north-east by the giants of the low hills after the Night of the Sea, long before Aen. The cairn at the head of the line, at Maruunos by the Giant River, holds the oldest stones of the count, and the giants paint its shape standing on water in ochre and blue on the great hide that hangs in the cairn-hall, because the line, they say, still holds back a sea. Dondor's chroniclers copied the shape from that hide after the woodcutters were carried back in 4A 1210.
sign.meaning: The line holds: the cairn promises that what the giants keep will never be breached again, and warns that whoever crosses it will be held back like the sea.

dynasties.name: The cairn-keepers of Maruunos
dynasties.notable: The oldest giant keeps the line of cairns, and the cairn-hall by the Giant River is his seat; the present keeper is called Dorunas by men, who have never heard him say his name.

events.name: The Carrying of the Stones
events.summary: After the Night of the Sea the giants of the low hills carried the stones of the broken dikes north-east, one under each arm, and raised them again as a line of cairns that is not to be crossed.

events.name: The Carried Woodcutters
events.summary: Dondor woodcutters who crossed the cairn-line were carried back over it by the giants, the first meeting men recorded.

events.name: The Broken Cairn
events.summary: Orcs of the Darks broke a cairn of the Borderline for its stone; the giants came out and broke the orcs' hold in return, and no one has touched a cairn since.

events.name: The River Gift
events.summary: A flood of the Giant River drowned the lower Dondor plain; the giants were seen carrying folk from the water, and then they went back into the forest.

countries.capitalReason: Maruunos, the river-seat, is the cairn-hall by the Giant River where the line of cairns begins; the oldest giant keeps the line from where it starts.
countries.today: A few hundred giants keep the low hills beside the Giant Forest behind the Borderline of Giants. They never attack first, and whoever crosses the cairn-line has them as an enemy.

divergence.what: An army crosses the cairn-line in the last war.
divergence.consequence: The giants join any war against the crosser, and the forest becomes a wall for its enemies.

divergence.what: The cairn-keeper opens the forest once to a realm that has kept the line.
divergence.consequence: That realm can cross the Giant Forest by the giants' own road, a passage no other army has.

divergence.what: The cairn-keeper lets a realm that has kept the line read the oldest stones at its head.
divergence.consequence: The giants' count can be laid beside the counts kept elsewhere, the heirs of the drowned land learn that the giants of the low hills still live, and the Forgotten Giants are forgotten no longer.

countries.name: The Darks

founding.story: The orc holds of the Dark Forests and the ogre clans of the caves under the Hills of Dark had raided each other for centuries until in 4A 1222 a hard winter drove both to the edge of starving, and the orc chief Grimduth went into the ogres' caves with meat instead of spears. The four forest holds and the ogre clans made one moot at Notdertu, where orc chiefs and ogre clan-heads sit together, and the orcs have had the ogres' strength beside them since.

roots.story: The orcs of the Dark Forests and the ogres of the caves under the Hills of Dark tell two different stories of where they came from, and the moot at Notdertu keeps both. The forest holds say their forebears were among the bands that came home from Dardan and found the iron hills full, and went into the Dark Forests' shade because nobody else wanted it. The ogres say their clans walked from the sunrise long before Aen, from lands where their kin still live on the far side of a sea, and came into the caves of the Darkness because the caves were dark and full of meat; nobody can test it, and the scholars of other lands note only that ogres live on both sides of the eastern seas. For centuries the two raided each other, until the hard winter of 4A 1222 left both starving and the orc chief Grimduth walked into the ogres' caves with meat on his spear and its point turned to the ground. The ogre clan-heads ate with him, and the Meat Moot was made. Everything the Darks are comes from that meal: at Notdertu every spear is grounded point-down before the moot sits, meat is shared before words, and nothing is decided until the orcs and the ogres both agree. The moot also carries one shame, the Broken Cairn of 4A 1483, when orcs of the holds broke a cairn of the giants' Borderline for its stone and the giants broke their hold, and it has forbidden its people to touch a cairn since. In 4A 1748 the orcs need the ogres' strength and the ogres need the orcs' hunting, and every envoy who would buy one without the other finds the spear still point-down.

sign.device: The Grounded Spear: a black spear turned point-down, its shaft wound with a white thong, on blood-red, with a black hem.
sign.origin: Grimduth carried meat into the ogres' caves on a spear turned point-down in the hard winter of 4A 1222, so that the ogres would see food before they saw a weapon, and the ogre clan-heads took the meat off the point. The spear is kept at Notdertu with its shaft still wound in the thong that tied the meat, and the moot sits only after every spear in the hall has been grounded the same way. The Darks' war-bands carry the grounded spear on red so that both peoples march under a sign both of them made.
sign.meaning: The moot's peace: orcs and ogres share before they speak, and the spear promises that the two peoples will not turn on each other, while warning outsiders that a point can be lifted.

dynasties.name: The moot of the four holds
dynasties.notable: Four orc chiefs and the ogre clan-heads sit in one moot; the orcs speak for the holds and the ogres for the caves, and nothing is decided until both agree.

events.name: The Meat Moot
events.summary: Grimduth brought meat to the ogre caves in a hard winter, and the orc holds and the ogre clans formed one moot at Notdertu.

events.name: The Broken Cairn
events.summary: Orcs of the Darks broke a cairn of the giants' Borderline, and the giants broke their hold in return.

events.name: The Cairn Law
events.summary: After the giants broke the hold whose orcs had broken a cairn of the Borderline, the moot at Notdertu forbade its people ever to touch a cairn again.

events.name: The Hunting Ground
events.summary: The moot agreed with Dondor which part of the Dark Forests each would hunt, the first agreement between the Darks and the men of the plain.

countries.capitalReason: Notdertu is the forest hold at the foot of the Hills of Dark, between the orcs' forest and the ogres' caves, the one place both peoples could meet on even ground.
countries.today: About sixty thousand orcs and ogres live in the Dark Forests' band and the Hills of Dark under their moot. The ogres are few, strong and meat-eating, and the orcs need their strength.

divergence.what: The moot hires its ogres to Goldoroth's host.
divergence.consequence: The warkingdom gains the strongest warriors of the Dark Lands, and the Darks gain meat for a hard winter.

divergence.what: The orcs and the ogres quarrel and the moot breaks.
divergence.consequence: The Dark Forests fall back into raids between holds and caves, and Dondor's northern forest is a battlefield again.

divergence.what: The moot rebuilds the Broken Cairn with its own hands and carries the stones back over the line.
divergence.consequence: The giants' grudge against the Darks ends, and a war that crosses the Borderline finds the Darks and the giants standing on the same side.

countries.name: Skragdurg

founding.story: The Fonoor Forest is the timber of the Dark Lands' straits, and the orcs who felled it and burned its charcoal were scattered camps until in 4A 1120 their chiefs built a hold at the forest edge of Gollonlon and named it the forest-hold. Since then Skragdurg has sold timber and charcoal to every shipwright on the straits, whatever master they serve.

roots.story: Skragdurg's chiefs say the forest-hold began with a tree nobody dared to cut. The Fonoor Forest has given timber to the straits since the Raiding Years of the Second Age, when the iron holds' raiders built their boats from it to cross the Northern Dark Strait; but at the forest's edge where Gollonlon now stands grew the Old Black, a tree so wide that its shade kept the sun off the felling camps all summer, and the camps held that the forest would take its revenge on whoever felled it. In 4A 1120 a chief called Grashdug cut it down with his own axe in a single season, and when no revenge came the camps followed him and built the forest-hold around the stump. The axe is still bitten into the stump at Gollonlon, and every chief must fell a great tree with his own hands before he may swear on it. From that felling comes the hold's character: the forest-hold cuts what others fear to, sells to anyone who pays and takes no side, because its people say the timber does not care which hull it becomes, and the charcoal-burners of Colost swore the same oath on the stump when they joined the hold in 4A 1350. It also comes with a fear the orcs do not say aloud, that the forest has not yet taken its revenge, which is why the hold plants a sapling for every great tree it fells and never cuts within sight of the giants' cairns. In 4A 1748 Skragdurg sells the timber for the Accord's ships and for Goldoroth's in the same season, and both sides suspect it of laughing at them.

sign.device: Grashdug's Axe: a broad felling axe bitten into a black tree-stump, iron-grey and black on charcoal-red, with a black hem.
sign.origin: The stump of the Old Black still stands at the forest's edge at Gollonlon with Grashdug's axe bitten into it, where he left it in 4A 1120 when the tree came down. Every forest-chief swears on the stump with his hand on the haft, and the axe is never drawn out, because the hold believes that the day it comes out the forest will take its revenge. The felling camps branded the axe in the stump on Skragdurg's timber long before anyone sewed it, and shipwrights on both sides of the straits know it as the mark of good timber.
sign.meaning: We cut what others fear: the axe promises timber to every buyer and warns that Skragdurg has already done the one thing everyone said could not be done.

dynasties.name: The forest-chiefs of Gollonlon
dynasties.notable: Chiefs who hold the forest-hold until challenged; each chief must have felled a great tree with his own axe.

events.name: The Forest-Hold
events.summary: The timber and charcoal camps of the Fonoor Forest built the hold at Gollonlon.

events.name: The Felling of the Old Black
events.summary: Grashdug felled the Old Black, the tree whose shade the felling camps feared to lose, and left his axe in the stump; the camps built the forest-hold around it.

events.name: The Colost Charcoal
events.summary: The charcoal-burners of Colost joined the forest-hold, and Skragdurg's charcoal began to feed the forges of the iron hills.

events.name: The Strait Hulls
events.summary: Skragdurg sold the timber for the Accord's new ships and the timber for Goldoroth's in the same season.

countries.capitalReason: Gollonlon stands at the Fonoor Forest's edge where the felled timber can be dragged down to the strait, the one place where forest and water meet.
countries.today: About sixty thousand orcs of the Iron Clans fell timber and burn charcoal in the Fonoor Forest with Colost, selling to every shipwright on the straits.

divergence.what: Skragdurg sells its timber to one side only in the last war.
divergence.consequence: That side's ships are built and the other's are not.

divergence.what: Skragdurg bows to the Iron Yoke.
divergence.consequence: Goldoroth gains the timber of the straits and can build a fleet for the Sea of Darkness.

divergence.what: A forest-chief draws Grashdug's axe out of the stump to arm the hold for war.
divergence.consequence: The felling camps believe the forest's revenge has begun, half of them leave the hold, and Skragdurg's neutrality ends with whoever the chief chose to fight for.

countries.name: Dun

founding.story: The eastern peninsula commands the mouth of the Dun Sea, and in 4A 1300 an orc chief named Rukhesk of the Zhaggul took the toll-town of Dobudo and called himself king of the peninsula. His heirs have lived on the Dun Sea's tolls since, and they swing to whichever neighbour pays best, which has made them the least trusted crown of the Dark Lands.

roots.story: The toll-kings of Dun claim a crooked ancestor and are proud of him. The Zhaggul say their forefather was an orc ship-captain of the First Age who sold the Grand Alliance the hour of Volgan's crossing and sold Volgan the hour of the Alliance's, took gold from both, and was paid by neither when they found out; whether it is true nobody can say, and the chroniclers of other lands have never found his name, but every Zhaggul child learns it. The peninsula at the mouth of the Dun Sea suited that lesson. Every ship into or out of the inner channel passes under Dobudo's walls, and when Rukhesk of the Zhaggul took the toll-town in 4A 1300 he set up the custom his house has kept since: the toll-king's ship flies a sail of two halves, each dyed in the colour of a neighbour who pays, and the halves are turned on the yard whenever the payment changes, so that the paymaster's colour faces the channel. The toll-kings marry into every hold that will have them, the crown goes to the son or daughter who wins the ring, and the house's law is that a promise lasts as long as its price, which made the Swing of 4A 1596 a matter of pride at Dobudo and of disgust everywhere else. From the ancestor's tale also comes the Zhaggul fear that a buyer who learns he has been sold will one day come back, which is why Dobudo's walls are the strongest on the Dun Sea. In 4A 1748 Dun is the least trusted crown of the Dark Lands and perhaps the best informed.

sign.device: The Turned Sail: a black ship with one square sail split down the middle, red on one half and white on the other, on a sea-grey field with a black hem.
sign.origin: The turned sail has been the toll-king's ship-sign since Rukhesk took Dobudo in 4A 1300: a sail of two halves, each dyed in the colour of a paying neighbour, turned on the yard whenever the payment changes. Ships entering the Dun Sea look at the toll-king's mast to know which side the channel favours that season. The red and white sewn on Dun's banner are the colours of the first two neighbours the Zhaggul sold the channel to, and the toll-kings like to say they have never needed a third.
sign.meaning: Everything has its season and its price: the sail promises any buyer the channel for a time, and warns everyone that Dun's favour turns with the wind.

dynasties.name: The Zhaggul toll-kings
dynasties.notable: Descended from Rukhesk; the crown goes to the son or daughter who wins the ring, and the toll-kings have married into every hold that would have them.

events.name: The Captain's Double Price
events.summary: The Zhaggul hold that their forefather, an orc ship-captain, sold the hour of Volgan's crossing to the Grand Alliance and the Alliance's to Volgan, and was paid by neither; the tale is their house's boast and nobody else's record.

events.name: The Toll-Town Taken
events.summary: Rukhesk of the Zhaggul took Dobudo and made himself king of the Dun peninsula.

events.name: The Dunbulinor Tolls
events.summary: The toll-gatherers of Dunbulinor were brought under the crown, and the whole mouth of the Dun Sea paid one king.

events.name: The Swing
events.summary: Dun took Goldoroth's gold to close the Dun Sea to Dondor, then Dondor's to open it again, inside one year.

countries.capitalReason: Dobudo is the toll-town on the Dun Sea's mouth, where every ship into or out of the inner channel passes under its walls.
countries.today: About fifty thousand orcs of mixed holds live on the Dun peninsula with Dunbulinor under a toll-king who sells his favour by the season.

divergence.what: The toll-king closes the Dun Sea to one side in the last war.
divergence.consequence: That side's ships cannot use the inner channel, and Dun names its price for opening it.

divergence.what: Goldoroth or Dondor takes the peninsula.
divergence.consequence: The Dun Sea's tolls go to a great power, and the Dark Lands lose their swing crown.

divergence.what: A power the toll-king sold in the last war comes back for Dobudo when the war is over.
divergence.consequence: The swing crown is besieged by the buyer it cheated, and the Dun Sea's tolls go to whoever takes the strongest walls on the inner channel.

countries.name: Britadon

founding.story: The iron hills of the south-east coast had been dug by small orc holds for centuries, and in 4A 1380 the chief of the hill hold at Fontadon, Bredesk of the Brakgul, brought the headland hold of Beriath under his iron and made one hold of the coast. Britadon has sold its iron by sea ever since.
